cues.say: A connection pooler is a small server that sits between your app and Postgres. It keeps a few real database connections open, and shares them among all your server copies.
The classic one is PgBouncer. Clouds offer managed ones too, like Amazon RDS Proxy.
First, what's a connection? It's an open line from your app to the database. Postgres runs a separate process for each one, so it can only afford a few hundred. The default limit is one hundred.
Each server copy keeps its own set open, say twenty, so it doesn't have to open a new one for every request. Add copies, and the count multiplies.
Past the limit, Postgres refuses new connections. Copy six can't connect, and its requests fail.
The pooler fixes this. Every copy connects to the pooler instead, and those connections are cheap.
Behind it, the pooler keeps a small set of real connections to Postgres.
When a copy runs a transaction, the pooler lends it a real connection, for just the milliseconds it takes, then puts it back.
Why are a few enough? If a query takes five milliseconds, one connection can run two hundred a second. Fifty connections: ten thousand a second.
So you need one as soon as you add copies of your API.
And whenever many short-lived workers or functions each want their own connection.
Now a real case. Before the game, the pizza shop scales from two copies to twenty, with twenty connections each. That's four hundred connections.
Their database allows two hundred. Copies one to ten connect. Copies eleven to twenty can't, and fail right at kickoff.
With a pooler, all twenty copies connect to it, and it keeps fifty real connections. The database stays well under its limit.
Here's where it sits: between your API copies and Postgres. Every query goes through it.
Two things to know. Keep transactions short. Never wait on Stripe while holding a connection, or the pool runs dry.
And each transaction may get a different real connection, so don't rely on settings that live in one session.
In the interview, say: Postgres allows a few hundred connections. Without a pooler, scaling the API takes down the database.
